podcast.title: Background and Mental Health
podcast.body: Wesley Willis was a 6'5", 350 lb street artist from Chicago who began showing signs of schizophrenia in 1989, leading to institutionalization. He had distinctive behaviors, including head-butting as a greeting (resulting in a perpetual forehead bruise), and struggled with hygiene and unexpected vomiting, yet found solace in music. "Wesley was a 6'5, 350 lb street artist from Chicago. His thing was selling landscape drawings to people who passed by on the street."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparison to Jimmy Mitchell
podcast.body: Jimmy Mitchell's style is noted to have similarities to that of Wesley Willis, suggesting a shared approach within outsider music. "If you're a student of outsider music, you might hear some of the similarities between his style and that of Wesley Willis, a performer covered on a previous episode on this subject."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death and Legacy
podcast.body: Wesley Willis's schizophrenia worsened over time, and he was later diagnosed with leukemia, which led to his death in August 2003. A large memorial service was held for him, and he continues to be regarded as a true outsider music superstar due to his prolific output and unbridled passion. "Sadly, Wesley schizophrenia became worse and then he was diagnosed with leukemia and he died in August of 2003."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Distribution
podcast.body: Friends helped Wesley form The Wesley Willis Fiasco, which toured with various indie bands. His recognition grew to the extent that he secured a record deal with Rick Rubin's American Recordings, providing major label distribution for some of his material, a rare achievement for an outsider artist. "He even picked up a record deal with Rick Rubin's American recordings, which means he actually had major label distribution for some of his material."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mention in Outsider Music History
podcast.body: Wesley Willis is listed among artists previously covered as examples of outsider music, alongside The Shags, The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, and others. "On those programs, I covered Wesley Willis, the Shags, the legendary Stardust cowboy, Jandic, Captain B. Fart, Daniel Johnson, Florence Foster Jenkins, and even Charles Manson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Music as Liberation
podcast.body: Music, particularly rock n' roll which he affectionately called his "joy ride music," served as a significant source of liberation for Wesley Willis from what he referred to as his "mental hell rides." He composed and sang passionately, typically using a cheap Technics electronic keyboard. "But one of the few things that liberated him from what he called his mental hell rides was music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Support from Indie Musicians
podcast.body: Indie musicians in Chicago and beyond, including producer Steve Albini and a former bandmate of Billy Corgan from a pre-Smashing Pumpkins band, took notice and supported Wesley. The Canadian industrial metal band Monster Voodoo Machine recorded with him, and Eddie Vedder was charmed by his work. "The indie musicians of Chicago and beyond took note, and they took a liking to him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mental Illness and Early Career
xref.body: Daniel Johnston has openly dealt with manic depression and schizophrenia, experiencing "buds of delusion" that raised genuine fears for his safety and that of others. He began his recording career by making cassettes on a $59 Stenial Boombox and gained attention by distributing them to everyone he met under his self-operated label, Stress. "Like Wesley Willis, Daniel has said to deal with mental illness. Manic depression and schizophrenia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
